newsitem.title: ICELAND: Iceland braces for deluge, scientists seek data.
newsitem.headline: Iceland braces for deluge, scientists seek data.

text.p: Icelanders living in the shadow of an erupting volcano awoke on Friday to the stench of sulphur, but fears that it heralded an expected massive flood of glacial water seemed to be premature.

The crater under the giant Vatnajokull glacier, on Iceland's southeast coast, began to spew ash and steam on September 30. The eruption has burst through the glacier and melted parts of the ice cap, causing billions of tonnes of water to accumulate in a nearby subglacial lake.
The water is threatening to break through the ice and cause massive flooding on the black sand plains below.

When residents of the village of Kirkjubaejarklaustur, about 75 km (45 miles) west of the glacier, smelled the foul odour, known locally as glacial stench, they took it as a first sign that the deluge was about to happen.
Scientists monitoring the flow of rivers and tributaries down Europe's biggest glacier saw no fresh signs of an impending flood, however, and said the odour was probably a false alarm.
A more likely explanation for the smell was that it came from the eruption after a change in wind direction.

"It is very unlikely this was due to the flood beginning. The water levels in the sand plains were the lowest measured since the start of the eruption," said Arni Snorrason, a hydrologist based at Skaftafell.
On Friday a huge column of white steam hung over the glacier, which had gathered a fresh sprinkling of snow overnight.
While Iceland held its breath, one British scientist said the current sub-glacial eruption was giving the scientific world new insights into the interaction of ice and fire,

"This is probably one of the most exciting eruptions since Mount St Helens in Washington State in 1980," Gillian Foulger, a geophysicist at the University of Durham in Britain, told Reuters in a telephone interview on Friday.
"The eruption has very unusual characteristics which could teach us something new and which may have implications for our understanding of volcanic behaviour worldwide." she said.
Foulger said it was one of very few instances where scientists had been able to study closely the interplay between volcanoes and glaciers.
She is leading a joint British-American-Icelandic study, the "Icelandic Hotspot" project, which has set up a network across Iceland to measure earth movements due to volcanic activity.
The project, costing a total of 500,000 pounds ($320,000), is funded jointly by British and American scentific institutes.
Iceland is one of the world's so-called "hot spots" for volcanic activity along with Yellowstone in California and Hawaii, Foulger said.
One of the seismic stations set up next to the Vatnajokull eruption site in August had provided invaluable data, she said.
"This equipment has provided us with the best data about any eruption ever anywhere in the world."
